content:
I'm pleased to announce a project I've been working on to make it easier to read and understand Lean libraries: Referee.

Referee lets you build a website for a Lean library that helps you understand what its theorems mean.

Say that you are looking at a Lean library and want to know what is proved in there. One way to do that is to read the code. That's many thousands of lines of code leading to any interesting theorem, which is impractical. But to understand that theorem you don't need to read any proof (you know those are checked), you just need to understand the statement. That statement depends on other definitions that you also need to read, which leads to a minimal "meaning dependency graph" for the theorem.
Referee computes that graph and guides you through it.

Two examples:

  • Referee for AlphaRAR, an AI auto-formalization of my latest preprint, for which the code is available here. See the formalization.yaml file in that repo for more context. Beyond checking my paper (and finding and fixing an error in the process), its goal it to serve as test bed for Referee.
  • Referee for LeanMachineLearning, a library of machine learning theory in Lean (see here). That Referee website does not use all the features of Referee (see below).

This is an alpha and I will change it a lot. The texts on the pages are AI-generated (as is the entire codebase) and could be improved. I'm posting here in the hope that some people will try it out and tell me what features they find useful, what is not, and what is missing.
The main idea is to present information from the library itself, and that information should not go through layers of interpretation (so it does not for example call any LLM judge to assess the validity of a formalization).

Features

Meaning dependency graphs: Each declaration page has a graph of the things you need to read in the repository to understand what it means. That graph ignores things used in proofs.
On LeanMachineLearning, reading only 10% of the declarations is enough to understand all the main theorems.
The website also gives a link to a minimal file (similar to a challenge file for Comparator) for each declaration that contains only the meaning dependency graph declarations.

See an example here.

Claims summary: the Claims page lists all theorems in the library. It assumes that the library uses theorem vs lemma in a meaningful way, and that theorems are the things you want to read. If the library does this, the claims page guides you towards the statements that matter.

See an example here.

Personalized audit: each declaration page lets you mark it as accepted or lets you record a question you have about it. The Audit page shows you what you have accepted, and what you still need to read to completely accept the dependencies of a claim. This is not shared with anyone else, it is just for you.

See an example here.

Characterization and specification attributes: the repository contains a separate library, LeanSpec, that defines two attributes to indicate that a lemma is part of the specification of a definition, or declare that something characterizes a definition (with some checks attached, see the docs). If your library uses these attributes, the declaration pages will show them.

See an example here.

Changes: the Changes page gives summaries of what changed between commits. It uses semantic_hash by @Adam Topaz to detect when the meaning of a declaration has changed, and when only the proof changed.

See an example here (select different commits to see the changes).

Several parts are optional: you don't have to use semantic_hash (and Referee does not depend on it) and you can choose to not track changes. Likewise, you don't have to use the new specifies and characterization attributes and the corresponding sections will not be shown if no attribute exists.

Note: packages

There are 3 libraries in this repo:

  • LeanDeps is the computation of the dependency graph data
  • LeanSpec defines the attributes specifies and characterization to help you write specifications for your definitions, and check that they are correct.
  • Referee is the main executable, which builds the site.

You repository can depend on LeanSpec to add the attributes to your code without depending on the rest of Referee. See the AlphaRAR repository for an example of how to do that.

I also built a Referee website for the Brownian Motion project. I mention this third example because it shows what happens if a declaration depends on sorry: example here (there is a note on the top right of the declaration card that says "depends transitively on sorry").
That library does not use the LeanSpec attributes so the website does not show any, and the library is not using theorem vs lemma in a principled way so the Claims page is not meaningful.
